claims.text: Thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr can be decomposed into lattice and electronic contributions.
A combined DFT, molecular-dynamics, and machine-learning framework can independently predict phonon and electronic transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Atomic-size and bond-length disorder in compositionally complex alloys produces local lattice distortion.
Chemical complexity in HfNbTaTiZr produces fluctuations in interatomic force constants.
Lattice distortion can alter electronic transport through changes in relaxation time, plasma frequency, effective mass, and free-electron density.
Explicitly isolating static lattice distortion from electronic scattering will accurately recover the distinct temperature dependences of phonon and electron transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr will remain nearly constant at approximately 4–7 W/(K·m) below 200 K.
The electronic thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr will have a mild temperature dependence.
Electronic thermal conductivity will become the dominant heat-transport contribution in HfNbTaTiZr above approximately 300 K.
For oxygen-free HfNbTaTiZr, total thermal conductivity will be 10–17 W/(K·m) from 300 to 1200 K.
The new framework will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 30% relative to previous Debye-based approaches.
Earlier Debye-temperature and mean-field approaches generally conflated lattice and electronic thermal conductivity.
Earlier approaches often overestimated lattice thermal conductivity and failed to reproduce its temperature dependence.
Electronic thermal conductivity can be estimated from electrical resistivity using the Wiedemann–Franz law and an assumed Lorenz number.
Wiedemann–Franz estimates may be less reliable at temperatures well below 300 K because the Lorenz number can deviate from its standard value.
The predictions apply to well-prepared, defect-free, single-phase bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
High defect densities, grain-boundary scattering, and non-ideal microstructures are expected to cause significant deviations from the predictions.
Minimal oxygen and other extrinsic impurities are required for measurements to represent intrinsic HfNbTaTiZr transport.

contradictions.description: The 10–17 W/(K·m) range is assigned specifically to oxygen-free samples and described as agreeing with key observations, while the conditions separately recognize oxygen-doped samples as potentially having shifted electronic contributions. No basis is given for transferring the oxygen-containing high-temperature range to oxygen-free material.

The baseline broadly characterizes earlier approaches as conflating lattice and electronic contributions, but the proposed falsification experiment itself relies on the established Wiedemann–Franz analytical separation used in cited prior work.
